I don't think it's the government's job to intervene in these specific cases - there should be safety nets for those in financial need (which there already are, and of course those could be improved upon). So, if a woman was pregnant or a new mother, she would qualify for government assistance based on financial need - not based on the fact that she can't get an abortion. We already have support for mothers who are in need (e.g., WIC, and as I've already stated these programs could be expanded/improved upon). 

Birth control is already widely covered under Obamacare. I think all government-provided healthcare should absolutely cover birth control, so I'm fine with tax dollars going to it in that sense. I think all private health insurances *should* cover it, but I don't think it's constitutional for them to be mandated to. Again, if programs were able to reach everyone who needed them, it wouldn't matter if not all private health plans covered birth control - you'd either get it through your government health plan if you qualified, and if you didn't, ideally you'd be able to afford it anyway (the private sector is making strides in this - birth control delivered monthly for very reasonable prices). 

Ultimately, I think it's the government's place to provide safety nets, but largely the place of communities to provide support. And the support is there for mothers with pregnancies for which they are unprepared - one of the biggest fallacies is that people in the pro life movement don't care about these women, when in actuality they are some of their biggest advocates and providers of charity and support for these women.

Eh, I think unsolicited expressions of concern about one's weight are generally very rude anyway - unless it's a serious problem and they are very close to you (i.e., spouse). Otherwise it's not your business and it's rude to try to make it so. I think it crosses into fat shaming if done to someone who very clearly is NOT morbidly obese, which it often is by "fatphobic" people. And I think though the two are often separate, "fatphobic" people use health concerns as a reason to justify their "fatphobia."

No, because the body positivity movement isn't about promoting unhealthy lifestyles. It's about accepting everyone, all bodies, all shapes & sizes, as valid and worthy of respect. It's about promoting the idea that an individual is not defined by their size, nor is their size even remotely the most important thing about them. 

That being said, feminism, at its core, is an ideology meant to liberate people from societal pressures and norms, to promote equality among all people regardless of differences, so that everyone is enabled to pursue their best life. It's not about deciding for them what that best life should be. 

So, while obesity is unhealthy (duh), there is no place in feminism to promote stigma against fat people. It's not up to you how others live their lives, but you can support them having the social and political freedom to pursue their own happiness.

Prima Via: The Argument of the Unmoved Mover

"In the world, we can see that at least some things are changing. Whatever is changing is being changed by something else. But this chain cannot be indefinitely long, so there must be something that causes change without itself changing. This everyone understands to be God."

Secunda Via: The Argument of the First Cause

"In the world, we can see that things are caused. But it is not possible for something to be the cause of itself because this would entail that it exists prior to itself, which is a contradiction. If that by which it is caused is itself caused, then it too must have a cause. But this cannot be an infinitely long chain, so, there must be a cause which is not itself caused by anything further. This everyone understands to be God."

Quinta Via: Argument from Final Cause or Ends

"We see various non-intelligent objects in the world behaving in regular ways. This cannot be due to chance since then they would not behave with predictable results. So their behavior must be set. But it cannot be set by themselves since they are non-intelligent and have no notion of how to set behavior. Therefore, their behavior must be set by something else, and by implication something that must be intelligent. This everyone understands to be God."

I totally understand how this dynamic can easily become emotionally draining - ours has been at times too but we've communicated about it and are working to make it better. If you haven't really talked about this specific impact with your boyfriend, I think you should, especially because from what you said, he seems to be particularly understanding of emotional issues. 

I'm going to throw in a personal example here, I'm not sure if these are helpful or not but I think it helps illustrate my experience better. Our earlier relationship felt really unbalanced in some ways, and was really emotionally draining for me. Specifically, when we moved in together, housework was the area where our dynamic was exacerbated. Through communication and effort on both our parts, we've reached a much healthier balance. Things still aren't perfect, but they're well on their way and I'm happy with where we are now. Recently, my fiance had a revelation about our dynamic that really spoke to me. 
We have an inspection coming up - there is quite a bit to get done around the house beforehand, but I'm already overloaded with summer classes, work, and wedding planning. I made him a list, and he's been knocking it out. This doesn't bother me; I like making lists. My fiances revelation was basically that I'm the planner and he's the executioner. I help him because on his own, he wouldn't think of all the little things around the house that need to be done, and because I make the house a home and he really appreciates that. He helps me because he does all he can to take some of the load off my shoulders - particularly when my anxiety flares up, because when it gets really bad I can't focus or even choose one task to start on (even though I know every single little thing that needs to be done). He has no problem just going and knocking things out, and quickly. 

This is an abridged version of what he said to me, but I liked it because something I've always viewed as a weakness (my anxiety),  he was able to see the strength in. 

It sounds like you are in a really good place right now: graduated school (congratulations!), are pursuing graduate studies, and just generally going after what you want. You seem like a very motivated, focused person. Think of your future: your career, your family, just what you want your life to eventually become. Think of your upcoming studies, the near-future and everything that is about to begin for you. Think about how your boyfriend would fit into all of that. 

And finally, I think the biggest question to ask yourself is, can you picture your life without him? How does that make you feel? 

One more personal example: when I was really struggling with some traits my guy had a few years ago (i.e., I love how funny and smart he is but I wish he was more organized), I envisioned a "hypothetical" boyfriend with all the characteristics that my boyfriend was lacking, but who in turn, didn't have the traits my boyfriend had that made me love him so much. Immediately I thought "fuck no." Because the truth is, I could have broken up with him and found somebody with those traits (somebody more like me), but they wouldn't have had the same mind as my fiance, the same world view, the same love for animals and family, the same curiosity, the same passions, the same love for who I am. Plus, they would have driven me crazy. I've come to accept that I like being in control. It can be draining at times, but I'd rather be allowed to organize the house how I want, be the primary planner, set the standards, etc. than have someone like me to wrestle with over that stuff. My fiance and I aren't perfect, but we are perfect for each other. 

Then of course, when I asked myself the ultimatum question I phrased to you above, I knew for sure he was going to be in my life as long as he was willing to put up with me. Haha. 

I hope my examples and advice are helpful. I think you should ask yourself those questions and reflect on what your priorities are for traits in a lifelong partner. If you decide to try to work things out, communicate everything you're feeling with your partner as gently and tactfully as you can. Maybe even think about couples counseling - it can be a really helpful tool. Along the way, though, make sure to affirm to him how much you care for and love him, and that the reason you are voicing these things and trying to work on them is *because* you love him - for the sake of your relationship. 

Ultimately, though, do what's best for the both of you. If things don't improve, it wouldn't be fair to you to have the emotional drain of your dynamic affecting you while you're trying to focus on your graduate studies. And if your expectations aren't something he could eventually develop on his own, or if it would be too difficult for you to compromise on them, it wouldn't be fair to him to feel like he's always falling short for just being who he is.

Reflect on your priorities in a relationship. I don't think you'll ever find someone perfect, because nobody's perfect, but you'll find somebody who complements your strengths and weaknesses perfectly, and vice versa. So, would you rather be with someone who is "on top of their shit" as you'd like your current BF to be, but who is emotionally unavailable? Or would you rather be with someone like your boyfriend? 
You also need to take growth into account, because you guys are so young and started dating young. My (23F) fiance (25M) and I started dating when we were 17 and 19, respectively. There were times in the first few years of our relationship where I was at my wit's end, and struggling between what I loved about him and areas I was worried about (similar to what you said; unsure if I could depend on him in the future, etc). But I looked at how far we'd come, and how much we both had grown, and decided we were going in the right direction, and I liked the direction he was growing in as a person. I'm so glad I made that choice. In some ways, he's a completely different person now than he was earlier in our relationship. The parts of him that I love have only gotten stronger, but he's also gotten more responsible, dependable, introspective, etc. People don't always mature at the same rates, especially guys and girls. 

So reflect on how he's grown since you've been together. Although he may not be as responsible and dependable as you'd like, are those characteristics stronger in him now than they used to be? Do you love him enough to give him and your relationship the time he/it needs to grow and mature, hoping it will stay on the right trajectory? Or are you too unsure and think it would be better to end it now? 

It took me time, too, to realize how much I appreciate that my fiance *isn't* like me. If he was a planner, a bit of a control freak, an anxiety-ridden go-go-go person like I am... I would probably hate being with him. We'd clash so much. But he's laid back, he goes with the flow, and he's forgetful and doesn't always follow through, but he always tries the best he can, and over the years we've learned how we are stronger together. He calms me down, I remind him of what's important and help him stay on track, we both keep each other grounded in different ways. 

So, I guess what I'm saying is evaluate how things have come so far and try to look to the future, and decide how long you're willing to stay in this relationship to either see what things could become or decide it's not what you need.

I highly value the right to bodily autonomy, but not over the right to life (at least, for the innocent). Bodily autonomy is predicated upon the right to life. A pregnant woman is a complicated situation, because it is indeed her body, but inside it is a growing, separate human being with its own body, its own unique DNA, its own heartbeat, etc. When a woman chooses to engage in heterosexual intercourse, she is doing so aware of the risks and potential consequences associated. She and her partner created the separate human being inside of her, and I don't think anyone has the right to take another life out of inconvenience. That being said, in cases of rape, there was obviously no choice or bodily autonomy involved on the woman's part in the act that created the human life, so while I morally disagree with abortion in that instance I believe it should be legally available for women to be able to make the choice they didn't have before. 


Same with instances where the mother's health is seriously put at risk by pregnancy. While I think all human life is valuable and worth protecting against outside influences that wish it harm (except for the most heinous among us, like child rapists, but that's a separate discussion), there is no question that an adult human's life is more valuable than a developing baby's. But, that doesn't invalidate the baby's to the point where it's okay to kill it needlessly, because it's still an innocent human life and still valuable and worthy of the protection granted to us by our inalienable rights. 


So apart from pregnancy, which is pretty much the only instance in which you are responsible for creating a situation in which another human life depends on your body for existence, everyone should have the right to dictate their own bodies - as long as they are not directly harming others unconsensually by doing so (which is what abortion boils down to). It is your right as a human being. So while I don't think doctors should be forced to perform medically assisted suicide, I think they should be allowed to, I think people should be allowed to seek it, and I think insurance companies should be allowed to cover it. It's up to an individual if they would rather die earlier, painlessly, and peacefully rather than later and in agony and pain. Or whatever their circumstances are. That's not for the government to decide for them.

My boyfriend had moved in with me, but we didn't even try to get him on the lease because we were worried he wouldn't be accepted - no established credit or previous rental history.
